answer: Yes. The subtext feels natural and enriches the story rather than forced. Q’s disintegrating napkin and slumped posture suggest the collapse of his controlled persona without requiring him to explain his feelings. The narrator’s refusal to approach him also implies that preserving an advantage over Q matters more to him than renewing their friendship, complicating his claim that this is the “truest” version of Q. The ordinary hotel-pool setting sharpens these tensions: a painful professional encounter unfolds amid shrieking children and flimsy snack-bar napkins, stripping Q’s apparent perfection of its protective surroundings.
